newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony, Toyota mulling joint LCD venture.
newsitem.headline: Sony, Toyota mulling joint LCD venture.

text.p: Japan's two big brand names, Sony Corp. and the Toyota Motor group, are discussing a plan to develop an electronics components business, expanding their already extensive reach into new fields.
Sony and Toyoda Automatic Loom Works Ltd, a unit of Toyota Motor Corp., said Wednesday they are considering forming a joint venture to produce next-generation liquid crystal displays.
LCDs are at present used mainly as displays for notebook computers. But they are expected to be widely used in desktop computers and TVs when prices come down.
"The idea is we may be able to combine Sony's know-how in LCD and Toyoda's manufacturing technology," a Sony spokesman said.
"We are discussing a possibility for a joint business," a Toyoda spokesman said, adding that an agreement could come in the near future.
Toyota, intent on finding new sources of income, recently made headlines with a plan, since dropped, to jump into profitable but risky computer memory chip production with Texas Instruments Inc.
Sony has developed a new type of LCDs, called polysilicon thin-film transistor LCDs, and is currently producing a small volume of the new type of LCDs for use in its video camcorders.
Sony said its technology allows production of large-size LCDs of about 20-inches, about twice the size of the panels used in notebook PCs, at low costs.
"The agreement, if it is reached, would mean Sony in full-fledged production of LCDs," the Sony spokesman said.
The financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said Sony and Toyoda plan to form a joint venture by the end of this year.

The two companies will spend 50 billion to 60 billion yen ($517 million) to build a factory in Aichi Prefecture in Western Japan that will start production as early as in the second half of the 1998/99 business year, the report said.
The Toyota group decided to enter the LCD business because the device may be used in cars in displays for navigation systems, the newspaper said.
Yoshiharu Izumi, analyst at UBS Securities, said he expects the market to balloon to around 300 billion yen ($2.58 billion) a year by 2000.
